title: Trails, Sizes, Clamps, Corners & Parameters
description: Four declarations that collapse something you used to spell out by hand, plus a scroll trail that animates numbers instead of elements.

drops.title: Ghost Trails
drops.description: Letters that remember where they have been, stroking their own past placements back out as outlined ghosts.
drops.concept: Codrops published a scroll-driven ghost-trail tutorial on 13 October 2026 whose real lesson is architectural: animate numeric values a renderer reads, rather than animating DOM elements directly. This reimplementation keeps that shape in plain Canvas 2D — each glyph owns a ring buffer of its past positions, and the ghosts are strokeText calls over those entries, so the trail is the actual motion history rather than offset copies. Scroll feeds one eased number; everything else falls out of it.
drops.source: Robert Aperios — “Typography That Leaves a Trace: Building Scroll-Driven Ghost Trails with GSAP” on Codrops

interaction.mouse: Scroll the page — the three rows travel their own sine paths and leave trails behind them.
interaction.click: Use the panel sliders to change ghost count, trail spacing, ripple amplitude and letter gap.
interaction.touch: Swipe to scroll; the rows keep breathing on their own when the page is still.

drops.title: One Declaration, Both Axes
drops.description: size, min-size and max-size set inline and block dimensions together — and they follow writing mode.
drops.concept: Safari Technology Preview 254 (8 October 2026) added the size, min-size and max-size shorthands. One value squares the box; two values read inline-then-block. The real payoff is logical sizing: min-width/min-height/max-width/max-height are four physical properties that break the moment a component is rotated, and these two shorthands survive it. The demo writes the real properties and carries a @supports-not fallback to the longhands, so it renders correctly either way and says in a live badge which path your browser took.
drops.source: WebKit — Release Notes for Safari Technology Preview 254

interaction.mouse: Hover the cards to lift them; watch the clamped card grow between its min-size and max-size.
interaction.click: Drag the panel sliders to drive width, height, min-size and max-size through custom properties.
interaction.touch: Cards reflow to a single column; the fallback path keeps the geometry identical.

drops.title: Clamping, Taken Apart
drops.description: The line-clamp shorthand split into continue, max-lines and block-ellipsis — so the marker is finally yours.
drops.concept: Igalia's explainer documents how CSS Overflow 4 decomposes line clamping into three longhands, and notes that Chromium's first implementation ships only the shorthand. Four cards each set a different one: the default ellipsis, a custom block-ellipsis string, no-ellipsis, and max-lines: auto clamping by height instead of by count. The @supports-not branch falls back to -webkit-line-clamp, which can count lines but cannot be told what to put at the end — which is the argument for the longhands, made visible.

interaction.mouse: Hover a card to lift it; compare the four clamp markers side by side.
interaction.click: Drag the lines slider to retarget max-lines across every card — the height-clamped card deliberately ignores it.
interaction.touch: The grid collapses to one column and the clamp behaviour is unchanged.

drops.title: Two Corners at a Time
drops.description: border-top-radius and its siblings own two corners each — so a transition stops dragging the other two along.
drops.concept: CSS Borders and Box Decorations Level 4 adds side shorthands for border-radius. Three interactions show why it matters in motion rather than in static styling: a tab that rounds into its panel, a sheet that squares its corners as it docks, and buttons that squish on one side when pressed. Animating one side used to mean animating the whole four-value shorthand, so untouched corners interpolated too — and any value you forgot to repeat snapped to zero mid-transition.
drops.source: W3C — CSS Borders and Box Decorations Module Level 4

interaction.mouse: Click the tabs to move the rounding, hover the frame to lift the sheet, and hold each button to squish it.
interaction.click: The radius slider retargets every demo at once through one custom property.
interaction.touch: Tapping a button fires its :active squish; focusing the frame lifts the sheet without a hover.

drops.title: One File, Six Themes
drops.description: An SVG declares its inputs with env(); the page fills them in with link-parameters — one cached asset, six palettes.
drops.concept: CSS Linked Parameters Level 1 lets a page pass values into a linked SVG, which decides how to use them: the asset declares named inputs with env() and their fallbacks, and the element supplies values with link-parameters: param(). Six img elements here share one identical data: URL and differ only in that declaration, next to the inlined-six-times workaround everyone ships today. Only Firefox Nightly and Safari Technology Preview implement it, so the top row shows the SVG's own fallbacks until it lands — which the page says out loud.
drops.source: Vadim Makeev — “One SVG, nine posters: CSS linked parameters”

interaction.mouse: Hover any poster to lift it; compare the shared-asset row against the inlined row below it.
interaction.click: Drag the hue slider — one custom property feeds both rows, through param() above and var() below.
interaction.touch: The poster grids reflow to fit; both rows stay in step.
